Given question: Julie Davies, a 26 year old woman, has just given birth to a baby boy. Julie's blood type is AB Rh negative, and her baby's blood type is AB Rh positive. In order to prevent haemolytic disease of the newborn (HDN) in her next child, what can Julie be given? Option A: Anti-D can be given within 72h after childbirth Option B: Anti-D can be given anytime to the mother within the next year Option C: Anti-D can be given to the mother when she decides to conceive again Option D: Pertussis vaccine is given to mother within 72h after childbirth Option E: Oxytocin is given to help speed up the afterbirth The correct answer is Option A.<turn|>
<|turn>model
chosen: Anti-D can be given within 72h after childbirth. Anti-D is an immuniglobuline that contains lots of IgG antibodies. If the mother is Rh negative and the foetus is Rh positive, during pregnancy there is a risk of the mother being sensitised to the Rh antigen of the foetus. It is thought that this is when the placenta is delivered, although it could occur at any time. Anti-D is given to the mother to destroy any Rh positive blood cells that may have entered her system. If the mother is sensitised, her body will start producing its own Rh antibodies, which will be found in her blood and in her breast milk. These antibodies can cross into the foetus through the placenta, and if the mother is sensitised, the foetus will be at risk of haemolytic disease of the newborn (HDN), where the foetal antibodies destroy the foetal RBCs.  Anti-D can also be given postnatally to prevent sensitisation to the Rh antigen of the baby that has just been born. It is important that the anti-D is given within 72h after childbirth, otherwise the mother will start producing her own antibodies, which will take some time to reach dangerous levels in the mother's blood. Pertussis vaccine is given to the patient at 28-32 weeks to protect the newborn baby from whooping cough. Oxytocin is given to help contract the uterus postnatally.
rejected: Anti-D can be given within 72h after childbirth to prevent sensitisation to Rh positive blood in the mother. Sensitisation occurs if the foetus is Rh positive and the mother is Rh negative as the foetal membranes are sometimes delivered before the baby (as is often the case with a C-section). If the mother is sensitised to Rh positive blood, then in a subsequent pregnancy of an Rh positive baby, anti-D can be produced which can cross the placenta and cause haemolytic disease of the newborn (HDN). HDN is caused by production of IgG antibodies to Rh antigens, which can cross the placenta and cause haemolytic disease of the newborn. Other antibodies, such as IgA antibodies, cannot cross the placenta and therefore will not cause HDN. Anti-D can also be given to the mother when she decides to conceive again to prevent sensitisation to Rh positive blood. Pertussis vaccine is given to mother within 72h after childbirth as part of the '1st Es' vaccination. Oxytocin is given to help speed up the afterbirth.

Given question: Denise has had COPD for around 10 years and has been coming to your clinic monthly. Recently she has started to gain weight and developed swelling around her ankles. She struggles to breathe and her alveolar ventilation is impaired.What does this ventilation directly depend on? Option A: Airway elasticity, compliance, resistance to air flow, tidal volume Option B: Airway radius, inspiratory reserve volume, resistance to air flow, respiratory rate Option C: Compliance, resistance to air flow, respiratory rate, tidal volume Option D: Distension of air ways, smooth muscle relaxation, resistance to air flow Option E: Distension of air ways, respiratory rate, respiratory rhythm, resistance to airflow The correct answer is Option C.<turn|>
<|turn>model
chosen: Ventilation refers to the movement of air in and out of the lungs. It is directly related to tidal volume and respiratory rate. Tidal volume refers to the air moved in/out of the lungs in quiet breathing and respiratory rate refers to the number of breaths taken per minute. Resistance to airflow refers to the friction that air meets when it moves through the airways. The greater the resistance to airflow the slower the rate of airflow and thus the less air that will move in and out of the lungs. Compliance refers to the ability of the lungs to stretch. The more compliant the lungs the more air that will be able to move in and out of the lungs. Tidal volume and respiratory rate are the two main determinants of alveolar ventilation.
rejected: Alveolar ventilation = what actually reaches the alveoli, i.e. gas exchange. It is different to minute ventilation which is the volume of air taken in and exhaled. Tidal volume = amount of air taken in and exhaled with each breath. Respiratory rate = number of breaths per minute. Compliance = ability of lungs to stretch. Resistance to air flow = how much the airways resist air moving in and out of the lungs.  COPD is an obstructive disease. This means that the airways are obstructed and so resistance to airflow is increased. This impairs alveolar ventilation. As Denise is struggling to breathe, she may be taking a bigger tidal volume, but there is a limit to how big it can be. She is also taking in more oxygen than she is using up, and this is contributing to her weight gain. This is because she is hyperventilation, and this means her blood vessels are dilating. This leads to her swelling up.
